body:
Mass spectrometry (MS) is arguably the most widespread
analytical technique in the history of science. MS spread from physics
(originating in the 1920s) to physical chemistry (1930s), to surface
science and geology (1950s), to organic chemistry (1960s), archeology
(1980s), environmental science (1970s), and finally to analytical
chemistry in the 1970s. This eventually paved the way for mass spectrometers
to be applied in biological science in the 1980s. Initial experiments
applying MS in the biological sciences focused on proteomics, but
it soon enabled metabolomics, and thus the entire emergence of the
-omics fields.
These applications were made possible by the
development of mass
spectrometers that sought to achieve different figures of merit: mass
resolving power, mass accuracy, linear dynamic range, sensitivity,
precision, efficiency (in ion transmission and duty cycle), speed,
cost, size, and ease-of-use. Interestingly, it took one hundred years
to get to the point where ease-of-use, reliability, instrument size,
and software development are now included as important analytical
figures of merit. These advancements are important because they enabled
mass spectrometers to be moved from academic laboratories, where the
instrument was used to explore fundamental aspects of physics and
chemistry, into the real world, and into the hands of people who are
making life-changing decisions in real-time, such as in newborn screening,
identifying inherited diseases, forensic applications, and environmental
monitoring.
While MS techniques have evolved, the field has
not abandoned its
fundamental roots. There are experiments that are still performed
under high vacuum and there are others developed to enable the noninvasive
analysis of samples in their native state, under more realistic conditions.
There are also experiments performed at pressures anywhere between
high vacuum and atmospheric pressure, as seen in ion mobility spectrometry
(IMS) experiments. Innovations that brought MS into the hands of more
users, including matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)
and electrospray ionization (ESI), also enabled mass spectrometers
to be coupled to other analytical techniques, including electrochemistry,
spectroscopy, microfluidics, and liquid chromatography (LC).
This
collection
highlights some of the diverse advances seen in new MS experiments
and techniques. The basic steps in a mass spectrometer involve ionization
and subsequent ion processing (i.e., measurement of mass-to-charge
and cross section of ion). The articles in this
collection
are grouped according to these fundamental steps, as well as the
advancement made by the study in terms of new concepts, methods, and
applications (
Tables
1
and
2
). The specific contributions (
not the title of the article
) are summarized as bold text
and placed under the graphical representations of the study. Reactions
are an integral part of MS experiments. As such, about one-third of
the selected articles developed new methods, concepts, and instruments
to advance various types of reactions, including plasma-induced epoxidation,
photoelectrochemical reactions, and photochemically induced nanoparticle
synthesis, all of which resulted in improved analytical performance.
Studies categorized under “hyphenation/integration”
combined reactions, chemometric tools, or separations with MS to achieve
new capabilities in chemical analysis and imaging.

In summary, this
collection
showcases new instrumentations, applications, concepts, and methods
in mass spectrometry, which are grounded in physical chemistry, surface
science, ion processing, ion reactions and organic chemistry, and
data processing. Demonstrated figures of merit ranges from ease-of-use,
to versatility, speed, sensitivity, and to complexity. Two notable
themes stand out in this
collection
: chemical reactions and chemometrics. These areas are expected to
have significant influence on the future of chemical measurements
by expanding the scope of application of existing MS instrumentation
without significant modification. Such opportunities are important
because it is by lowering the barriers of chemical instrumentation
that MS experiments can continue to spread to nontraditional fields,
such as in the validation of radiation dosage to be used in positron
emission tomographic (PET) measurements.
We hope that you enjoy
this Collection of stellar work on MS and
look forward to publishing more outstanding work on advances in MS
for years to come.
